question: Which statement best describes translate, scale, rotate, skew?
options: Multiple functions can be listed in one transform value and are applied right to left (the last one happens first in coordinate space), so order matters: translate then rotate differs from rotate then translate. Keep all transforms in a single declaration — a second transform property overrides the first rather than adding to it.

transform-origin sets the point an element transforms around — the pivot for rotation, the anchor for scaling, the reference for skew. It defaults to center (50% 50%) but can be any position (e.g. top left, 0 100%). Changing it dramatically changes how rotate and scale look.

Transforms come in 2D (translate, scale, rotate, skew) and 3D (translate3d, rotateX/rotateY/rotateZ, translateZ) variants. 3D transforms add depth and require a perspective on the parent (or perspective() in the value) to look three-dimensional, enabling effects like card flips and tilts.

The four core 2D transform functions: translate(x, y) moves an element along the axes, scale(x, y) resizes it (1 = original, 2 = double), rotate(deg) spins it around its origin, and skew(x, y) slants it. Each has axis-specific variants (translateX, scaleY, etc.) and percentage support for translate (relative to the element's own size).

Because transforms (and opacity) can be handled on the compositor thread, browsers often offload them to the GPU, animating them without recalculating layout or repainting. This is why transform-based motion stays at 60fps where top/left or width/height animations stutter. will-change: transform can hint the browser to promote the element to its own layer.

question: Which statement best describes Combining transforms?
options: A classic absolute-centering trick: position an element at 50%/50% then pull it back by half its own size with translate(-50%, -50%). Because translate percentages are relative to the element's own dimensions, this centers it perfectly without knowing its width or height.
